title: Module 13: The history and future of computers and the internet

spans.alt: Timeline from mechanical calculators to today's internet and possible future technologies
spans.caption: ENIAC, ARPANET, TCP/IP, the World Wide Web, and possible directions for the future

spans.text: Why were the first computers built?

People used tools such as the abacus and mechanical calculators long before electronic computers. These tools made arithmetic faster, but they could not carry out many different tasks automatically. By the twentieth century, science, engineering, and government needed large amounts of calculation. During wartime, preparing tables that predicted artillery-shell paths was one demanding example. Early computers were mainly built to perform large calculations faster and more consistently—not to write personal messages or browse the web.
ENIAC and the question “What was the first computer?”

ENIAC was built in the United States between 1943 and 1945 and introduced to the public in 1946. It was a very large, fast electronic digital calculating machine using vacuum tubes; one of its important jobs was producing artillery tables. Other mechanical, electromechanical, and special-purpose machines existed before and around the same time. So the answer to “first computer” depends on what we mean: electronic, programmable, general-purpose, or widely used. It is not accurate to call ENIAC the undisputed first computer. A careful description is that it was among the first large-scale general-purpose electronic digital computers.
The beginning of the internet: ARPANET

In the 1960s, researchers explored sending information between distant computers in small pieces called packets. The goal was to share computers and information across research centers and communicate over distance. The first computers on ARPANET, a network supported by the U.S. ARPA agency, were connected in 1969. In October that year, the first host-to-host message was sent from UCLA to SRI. During the first attempt, only “LO” from the word “LOGIN” arrived before the system stopped. It was a small experiment on the way to a working network. ARPANET was an important predecessor of today's internet, but it was not the whole internet we use today.
When did the internet begin, and what was it for?

The internet is not a single device built on one day. It is a way for separate networks to connect using shared rules. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to the TCP/IP protocols. This date is often treated as an important starting point for the modern internet, but the internet developed over many years. Its purpose was to let computers on different networks communicate and move data from a source to a destination. Those shared rules later made it possible to connect universities, businesses, public organizations, and home users around the world.
The internet and the Web are not the same thing

The internet is the underlying infrastructure and shared rules that connect devices and networks. The World Wide Web, or Web, is one of the services that runs over the internet: pages and resources that we open in a browser and connect with links. Tim Berners-Lee proposed the Web project at CERN in 1989; the first server and browser were ready in 1990, and the Web became available to others in 1991. Email and file transfer are other services that use the internet, but they are not the Web.

Today, data centers and cloud services work alongside phones, smart-home devices, and industrial equipment. AI assistants and edge computing can process some information on a device or a nearby server, so not every task needs to send everything to the cloud. Faster networks, robots, new medical tools, and quantum computing may develop further, but none is guaranteed to solve every problem or become common at the same time. Security, privacy, accessibility, energy use, and trustworthy information matter just as much as new features. IT professionals should consider a tool's benefits, risks, and effects on people together.
